group.title: Business terms
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A paper that lists what a customer must pay.
examples: Please send the {invoice} by email.
wrong: An invoice is a list of the books you want to read.
He invoice us for the work.

words.meaning: A written agreement between people or companies.
examples: Both sides signed the {contract}.
wrong: We signed the contract, but nobody agreed to anything.
She contract the new worker.

words.meaning: A person who watches and guides the work of others.
examples: My {supervisor} checks the schedule every morning.
wrong: A supervisor is a worker who watches nobody and guides no one.
She supervisors a team.

words.meaning: Extra hours of work after the normal day.
examples: I worked two hours of {overtime} last night.
wrong: I left work early, so I did a lot of overtime.
He overtimes yesterday.

words.meaning: A list of things to talk about at a meeting.
examples: The {agenda} has five items.
wrong: The agenda lists what we did last year, not what we will discuss.
She agendas many things.

words.meaning: The amount of work a person has to do.
examples: Her {workload} is heavy this week.
wrong: My workload is small because I have too much to do.
She workloads many tasks.

words.meaning: An amount of something that is available to use.
examples: The office has a good {supply} of paper.
wrong: We have a big supply, so we have no paper.
He supply of the shops.

words.meaning: A large building where goods are stored.
examples: The goods are kept in a {warehouse}.
wrong: I live in a warehouse for my bank account.
She warehouses in the town.

words.meaning: To talk in order to reach an agreement.
examples: We will {negotiate} the price with the supplier.
wrong: We negotiate when we refuse to talk to the other side at all.

words.meaning: A company or person that provides goods.
examples: Our {supplier} delivers fresh fruit every morning.
wrong: A supplier is a customer who buys goods from a shop.

words.meaning: A person who owns part of a company.
examples: Each {shareholder} voted at the meeting.
wrong: A shareholder is a person who does not own anything in a company and works there.

words.meaning: The joining of two companies into one.
examples: The {merger} created the largest bank in the country.
wrong: A merger is the splitting of one company into two, with no joining.

words.meaning: Money you make after paying all costs.
examples: The company made a large {profit} this year.
wrong: Profit is the money that a company loses.

words.meaning: The total money that a company receives from sales.
examples: Annual {revenue} reached ten million dollars.
wrong: Revenue is the money a company spends on its workers.

words.meaning: Money that you spend on something.
examples: Travel is a big {expense} for our team.
wrong: An expense is money that a company receives from customers.

words.meaning: To put money into something to get more money later.
examples: They plan to {invest} in a new factory.
wrong: I invest money when I put it in my pocket and spend it on lunch.

words.meaning: A plan for how to achieve a long-term goal.
examples: The company changed its {strategy} after the loss.
wrong: A strategy is a small detail you can forget.

words.meaning: A person or company that tries to do better than another.
examples: Our main {competitor} lowered its prices.
wrong: A competitor is a friend who works with you without any rivalry.

words.meaning: Unable to pay what you owe.
examples: The company went {bankrupt} after the crisis.
wrong: The company is bankrupt, so it has plenty of money and no debt.

words.meaning: To pay another company to do part of your work.
examples: Many firms {outsource} their customer service.
wrong: We outsource work when we do it all ourselves.

words.meaning: To start selling a new product to the public.
examples: The company will {launch} the app next week.
wrong: A company launches a product when it stops making it forever.

words.meaning: A person or group with an interest in a business or project.
examples: Every {stakeholder} was invited to the meeting.
wrong: A stakeholder is a person who has no connection with the project.

words.meaning: All the people who work for a company or in a country.
examples: The {workforce} grew by ten percent.
wrong: A workforce is a machine that makes coffee.

words.meaning: The amount of business a company does, or the rate at which workers leave.
examples: High staff {turnover} is expensive for a company.
wrong: Turnover is the amount of time that a worker spends asleep.

words.meaning: How much work a person or a machine does in a given time.
examples: New software improved {productivity}.
wrong: Productivity is the lack of any work done.

words.meaning: Working well without wasting time or energy.
examples: The new machine is more {efficient} than the old one.
wrong: The machine is efficient because it wastes a lot of energy.

words.meaning: To start using a plan or a system.
examples: The school will {implement} the new rules in May.
wrong: We implement a plan when we forget it and throw it away.

words.meaning: The final result of something.
examples: We were pleased with the {outcome} of the meeting.
wrong: An outcome is the beginning of something before anything happens.

words.meaning: Something that is more important than other things.
examples: Safety is our first {priority}.
wrong: A priority is something that is unimportant.

words.meaning: Something useful that a person or company can use.
examples: Time is a valuable {resource}.
wrong: A resource is a thing that nobody can ever use.

words.meaning: Something difficult that tests your ability.
examples: Learning a new language is a big {challenge}.
wrong: A challenge is an easy task that needs no effort.

words.meaning: To change in order to fit new conditions.
examples: Children {adapt} quickly to a new school.
wrong: We adapt when we refuse to change anything.

words.meaning: To work together with other people.
examples: The two teams will {collaborate} on the project.
wrong: People collaborate when they work separately and never talk.

words.meaning: To give part of your work to someone else.
examples: A good manager knows how to {delegate}.
wrong: A manager delegates when she does all the work alone.

words.meaning: To officially accept a plan or request.
examples: The board must {approve} the budget.
wrong: We approve a plan when we reject it completely.

words.meaning: To suggest a plan or an idea for others to consider.
examples: I {propose} that we meet on Friday.
wrong: I propose an idea when I refuse to say anything about it.

words.meaning: Something you plan to achieve.
examples: Our main {objective} is to reduce costs.
wrong: An objective is something that you have no plan to do.

words.meaning: An important stage in a project.
examples: Finishing the design was a major {milestone}.
wrong: A milestone is a small mistake that nobody notices.

words.meaning: A statement about what will probably happen.
examples: The sales {forecast} looks good for next year.
wrong: A forecast is a report about what happened last year.

words.meaning: An official check of a company’s accounts.
examples: The bank carried out an {audit} of the accounts.
wrong: An audit is a party for all the workers after a successful year.
